A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2323 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

Recent findings suggest that this unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

Sources indicate that the term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Recent findings suggest that although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

Recent findings suggest that the proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

Industry observers note that "In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the newly introduced approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Recent findings suggest that crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

It has been revealed that the first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

Industry observers note that according to the fresh research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

In a recent development, "Our study indicated that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

It has been revealed that ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

It has been revealed that the researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

In a recent development, "Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is crucial because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

According to recent reports, whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

Recent findings suggest that the nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

Recent findings suggest that "We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

Sources indicate that the weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially vital. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

Industry observers note that this fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

According to recent reports, "Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

Recent findings suggest that the approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

Industry observers note that the results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

Sources indicate that this makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely fresh materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain vital challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

Sources indicate that from the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study reveals how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising newly introduced way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands. Get the first one wrong and you can't win the dispute later, no matter how good your case is.

In this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP). Your code owns the data and the logic, and a thin adapter talks to Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com or whoever processes your payments.

Friendly fraud happens when a customer makes a real purchase, then disputes it with their card issuer. They might claim they didn't authorize it, that it never arrived, or that they canceled. Sometimes it's honest confusion. A spouse used the saved card, or the charge highlighted up under a name they didn't recognize. Sometimes it's a free refund with extra steps.

Recent findings suggest that either way, the money leaves your account. A dispute (also called a chargeback) reverses the payment, and your processor charges a dispute fee on top. Lose too many, and the card networks put your account into a monitoring program with higher fees.

It's also common. Visa puts friendly fraud at around 20% of fraudulent disputes globally, and up to 30% for high-volume online merchants. Mastercard goes further: it says first-party fraud makes up 75% of the fraud online businesses experience.

According to recent reports, so why is this your problem and not finance's? Because the evidence that wins these disputes is created at checkout, by your code. If your app never stored the customer's IP address, device ID or login history, nobody can produce it three months later when the dispute arrives.

Friendly fraud can be stopped at four points, and each one is a different piece of code:.

Industry observers note that most guides only cover stages 1 and 4. The rest of this tutorial walks through all four.

In a recent development, log four things on every order: the customer's IP address, a device ID, their account ID and the shipping address. Those are the data elements Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rules check when you fight an "unauthorized" fraud dispute.

It has been revealed that here's how CE3.0 works. You win the dispute if you can show two earlier, undisputed purchases on the same card, made 120 to 365 days before the disputed one. All three purchases must share at least two data elements, and one of them must be the IP address or device ID. In plain terms: same card, same person, same device, and they never complained before.

Most PSPs support CE3.0, including Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com and Airwallex. But none of them can submit data you never captured. And because the window reaches back a full year, you need to keep these logs for at least 13 months (Mastercard's rule, below).

In a recent development, mastercard has its own version, called First-Party Trust, for disputes filed under reason code 4837 (no cardholder authorization). It asks for one data point from each of three categories: a device factor (IP address, device ID or fingerprint), a delivery factor (shipping address, email or phone) and a different identity factor (such as account login ID or billing address). On the dispute route, Mastercard calls a lookup service that you host, with named fields such as deviceIpAddress, orderDeviceId, orderEmail and userIdName. That service has to answer in about 2.5 seconds on average and search 13 months of sales data.

Recent findings suggest that first-Party Trust is live in the US. Per Mastercard's October 2026 announcement, it reaches Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026 and the rest of Europe from July 2027. If you sell into Europe, the logging work is due now.

Two storage rules save you pain later:.

The good news: one evidence table serves both networks. Capture the data once, then keep the eligibility checks for Visa and Mastercard separate.

Start with a table that stores this data per order, separate from your PSP:.

Recent findings suggest that then capture it in your checkout route. If your app sits behind a proxy or CDN, set Express's trust proxy so req.ip returns the customer's address, not your load balancer's:.

According to recent reports, the psp object is your adapter: one small module per provider that maps its API to the same shape. Swap providers, and this route doesn't change.

For digital products and SaaS, log usage too. Login timestamps, downloads and feature activity prove the customer used what they paid for, which beats "I never received it" claims.

Recent findings suggest that the cheapest dispute is the one that never happens. Three checkout changes do most of the work: 3D Secure on risky payments, a billing descriptor customers recognize, and a few rules that stop obvious abuse.

Sources indicate that use 3D Secure where risk is higher. 3D Secure (3DS) asks the cardholder to confirm the payment with their bank, often through an app prompt. For authenticated payments, liability for fraud disputes generally shifts from you to the card issuer. Every major PSP supports it, and most let you request it per payment instead of forcing it on everyone. Forcing it everywhere adds friction and costs conversions, so trigger it on risk signals.

Make your billing descriptor obvious. The descriptor is the text on the customer's card statement. If it reads PMT*SRV 8812 instead of your product name, expect "I don't recognize this charge" disputes. Use the brand name customers know, and add a support URL or phone number where your PSP allows it. If you sell several products, use a dynamic descriptor that names each one.

Add a risk check before you charge. Most PSPs include a rules engine, but a small check in your own code keeps the logic portable:.

It has been revealed that store the signals array with the order. If a dispute arrives later, you'll know whether the payment looked risky at the time, which helps you decide whether to fight it or accept it.

According to recent reports, keep the rules few and specific. A rule that blocks 5% of good customers to stop 1% of bad ones costs more than the disputes it prevents.

Recent findings suggest that yes, if you ship physical goods. The window between a successful payment and the moment an order ships is the cheapest place to stop friendly fraud: nothing has left the warehouse, so canceling costs you nothing but the sale. Most fraud tools decide at checkout and never look again.

In a recent development, the pattern is a fulfillment gate. Instead of sending every paid order straight to your warehouse or 3PL, route it through a decision step first:.

The verify path does two jobs. Legitimate buyers confirm and their order ships. Buyers planning to dispute see that the store is watching, and a confirmed verification becomes evidence if they dispute anyway.

Industry observers note that the hard part is screenOrder. Your own data only highlights how a customer behaved with you. A buyer who has filed "item not received" disputes at 10 other stores looks brand new on their first order with yours. That's why post-purchase screening works best on shared data across many merchants.

According to recent reports, chargeflow Prevent is one example of this kind of friendly fraud prevention. It scores each order after checkout and before fulfillment, links device, IP, email and payment behavior across a network of 20,000+ merchants, and returns approve, verify or cancel. Today it runs as a Shopify app, with no checkout changes. A public Prevent API isn't available yet, so on other stacks you'd build the gate above with your own rules and data.

It has been revealed that build an order lookup endpoint. When a cardholder taps "I don't recognize this" in their banking app, the issuer can now ask the merchant for order details before a dispute is filed. Visa does this through Verifi Order Insight, and Mastercard through Ethoca Consumer Clarity. Show the customer a receipt with your logo, the items and the delivery date, and many disputes are never filed.

One endpoint can serve both networks, plus Mastercard's First-Party Trust dispute route. Mastercard's published service levels for this kind of lookup are strict:.

The tricky part is matching. Issuers often send partial data, so match on whatever arrives: acquirer reference number (ARN), authorization code, date, amount, currency, and card BIN plus last four digits.

On top of lookups, Visa and many PSPs offer rules-based auto-refunds. Verifi's Rapid Dispute Resolution (RDR) and Visa Resolve refund pre-disputes that match rules you set, such as "refund anything under $25". You don't write code for these, but you do pick the thresholds, so treat them like the REFUND_THRESHOLD below.

According to recent reports, if you sell subscriptions, many friendly fraud disputes aren't about stolen cards at all. The customer forgot about a renewal, couldn't find the cancel button, or thinks they canceled. Each of these has a code fix.

Here's a daily job that sends renewal reminders and records that each one went out:.

That evidenceLog row matters. When a customer later claims they never knew about the renewal, you can show the exact date you told them.

Sources indicate that automate two things: refunding payments that get flagged before they become chargebacks, and building evidence packets for the ones you fight. Both run off webhooks, and both have hard deadlines that humans miss.

Card networks can warn you before a dispute is filed. Visa runs this through Verifi and Mastercard through Ethoca, and many PSPs pass these alerts or their own early fraud warnings to you by webhook. Refunding at this stage costs you the sale, but you skip the dispute fee and the dispute doesn't count against your ratio.

Sources indicate that the threshold is a business call. Refunding a $20 order is cheaper than fighting it; a $900 order with strong evidence may be worth contesting.

When a fraud dispute arrives, check whether it qualifies for CE3.0 by looking for two earlier undisputed orders on the same card that share data with the disputed one:.

Recent findings suggest that if you get two matches, pass them to your PSP's CE3.0 evidence fields. On Stripe that's evidence.enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3; other PSPs have their own equivalents. Your adapter handles the mapping. If not, fall back to standard evidence: the IP, receipt, usage logs, renewal reminders and terms acceptance you've been logging all along.

According to recent reports, always submit before the deadline your PSP returns with the dispute. A late response is an automatic loss.

The code above covers the basics. A production system also needs evidence templates per reason code, network deadlines per card brand, retries, and win-rate tracking. That maintenance multiplies with every PSP you add.

Industry observers note that PSP-native tools only see that PSP's data, so they miss the usage logs, renewal reminders and support threads in your own app. A dedicated platform connects to your PSPs and lets you send that data in.

Here's what the buy path looks like with the Chargeflow API. Chargeflow ingests disputes from connected PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen, Checkout.com, Braintree and 20+ others), fires a dispute.created webhook, and you enrich the dispute with the evidence you logged:.

Chargeflow then builds the response and submits it to the PSP before the deadline. Pre-dispute alerts work the same way: Chargeflow can refund flagged transactions for you, or send alerts.created and alerts.transaction.linked webhooks so your code problems the refund and reports the result to POST /alerts/{id}/outcome.

Using Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to build this? Chargeflow publishes its whole developer documentation as one machine-readable file, docs.chargeflow.io/llms-full.txt. Point your assistant at it and it can write the webhook handler and field mapping against the real API, not a guess.

According to recent reports, then your merchants get the disputes, and you need to give them a dispute product without building a dispute team. Chargeflow Connect is built for this. It exposes the same prevention, alerts and recovery engine to your platform in a few delivery models:.

EaaS is the most developer-friendly entry point. You POST /public/2025-04-01/evidence with a merchant account_id and a dispute, get back an in_progress record, and receive an evidence.ready webhook with the PDF link, typically in about 30 seconds. Store the evidence id, not the URL, because the download link expires after 7 days. You can run it on auto-pilot (Chargeflow generates and submits) or co-pilot (your merchant approves first).

According to recent reports, don't wait for a customer to dispute a charge to find out your evidence pipeline is broken. Most PSPs give you test cards that create disputes on demand.

Sources indicate that one more check before launch: confirm your webhook endpoints verify signatures and return 200 fast. PSPs and Chargeflow retry deliveries that fail, and a slow handler can process the same dispute twice.

If you only do one thing this week, start logging IP address and device ID on every order. Everything else builds on that data.

True fraud is when a criminal uses a stolen card. Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes a purchase, then disputes it. Prevention differs: true fraud is stopped at checkout with risk checks and 3DS, while friendly fraud is won with evidence after the fact.

Mostly, yes. Both describe a real cardholder disputing a legitimate charge. "Chargeback fraud" usually implies the customer did it on purpose, while friendly fraud also covers honest mistakes, like a forgotten subscription or a family member's purchase. Visa calls it first-party misuse, and Mastercard calls it first-party fraud.

Sources indicate that check the reason code first. For "unauthorized" fraud claims, submit Visa CE3.0 or Mastercard First-Party Trust evidence if the customer qualifies. For "not received" or "canceled" claims, submit delivery proof, usage logs and your cancellation records. For low-value orders, accepting the dispute or refunding on an alert is often cheaper than fighting it.

No. CE3.0 needs two undisputed purchases on the same card made 120 to 365 days earlier, so it only protects returning customers. For first-time buyers, rely on 3DS and standard evidence.

Yes. Mastercard's First-Party Trust program covers reason code 4837 disputes. It needs one device, one delivery and one extra identity data point, and Mastercard checks them against the cardholder's past purchases. The same evidence table you build for Visa feeds both.

In a recent development, it depends on the stage. At checkout, your PSP's 3D Secure and rules engine. After payment, post-purchase screening such as Chargeflow Prevent holds risky orders before they ship. Before a chargeback, Verifi Order Insight and Ethoca Consumer Clarity show cardholders the order details, while Verifi and Ethoca alerts (offered by many PSPs and by Chargeflow Alerts) and RDR let you refund early. After a chargeback, Visa CE3.0, Mastercard First-Party Trust and dispute automation tools submit the evidence. For developers, the Chargeflow API covers the alert and dispute stages across PSPs, and Chargeflow Connect does the same for platforms.

Breaking: Falcon-H1: A Family of Hybrid-Head Language Models Redefining Efficiency and Performance

📅 21 May 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today, we are proud to introduce the Falcon-H1 series, a collection of six open-source models ranging from 0.5B to 34B parameters, each available in both base and instruction-tuned variants.
  • In this release, we feature six open-weight models: 0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-Deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B, along with their instruct versions.
  • Hybrid Architecture (Attention + SSM): We combine attention and Mamba-2 heads in parallel within our hybrid mixer block.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check out also our official blogpost.

Recent findings suggest that today, we are proud to introduce the Falcon-H1 series, a collection of six open-source models ranging from 0.5B to 34B parameters, each available in both base and instruction-tuned variants. At the core of these models lies a hybrid architecture that combines the strengths of the classical Transformer-based attention mechanism with the State Space Model (SSM), known for its superior long-context memory and computational efficiency. This architectural innovation is further enhanced by fundamental advancements in training dynamics and data utilization, enabling Falcon-H1 models to deliver uncompromised performance that rivals the top Transformer-based models across all covered size tiers.

In this release, we feature six open-weight models: 0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-Deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B, along with their instruct versions. All our open-source models are with a permissive license based on Apache 2.0.

Hybrid Architecture (Attention + SSM): We combine attention and Mamba-2 heads in parallel within our hybrid mixer block. Importantly, the amount of attention and mamba heads can be adjusted independently, allowing for an optimal attention/SSM ratio. This hybrid design enables faster inference, lower memory usage, and strong generalization across tasks.

Wide Range of Model Sizes: Available in six scales—0.5B, 1.5B, 1.5B-deep, 3B, 7B, and 34B—with both base and instruction-tuned variants, suitable for everything from edge devices to large-scale deployments.

Multilingual by Design: Supports 18 languages natively, including Arabic (ar), Czech (cs), German (de), English (en), Spanish (es), French (fr), Hindi (hi), Italian (it), Japanese (ja), Korean (ko), Dutch (nl), Polish (pl), Portuguese (pt), Romanian (ro), Russian (ru), Swedish (sv), Urdu (ur), and Chinese (zh) — with scalability to 100+ languages, thanks to our multilingual tokenizer trained on diverse language datasets.

Compact Models, Big Performance: Falcon-H1-0.5B delivers performance on par with typical 7B models from 2024, while Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep rivals many of the current leading 7B–10B models. Each Falcon-H1 model is designed to match or exceed the performance of models at least twice its size, making them ideal for low-resource and edge deployments without compromising on capability.

256K Context Support: Falcon-H1 models support up to 256K context length, enabling applications in long-document processing, multi-turn dialogue, and long-range reasoning.

Exceptional STEM capabilities: Falcon-H1 models deliver strong performance in math and science domains thanks to the focus on high-quality STEM data during training.

Robust Training Strategy: Uses a high-efficiency data strategy and customized Maximal Upgrade Parametrization (μP) to ensure smooth and scalable training across model sizes.

It has been revealed that when embarking on the Falcon-H1 series development, we chose to fundamentally rethink the training approach. While the field of LLM development has converged on many established practices that reliably produce strong models, these conventions were primarily validated on classical transformer architectures. The shift from pure attention mechanisms to a hybrid attention-SSM design represents a significant architectural change, making it uncertain whether these standard practices would remain optimal.

Given this uncertainty, we conducted an extensive experimentation phase, systematically revisiting nearly every aspect of model design and training methodology before launching our final training runs. While we will provide comprehensive details in our upcoming technical report, we'd like to share the key insights that shaped the Falcon-H1 models.

The hybrid attention-SSM models have a larger configuration space of all the parameters that define the model architecture. Our goal was to probe each of these configuration parameters to check its impact on model performance and efficiency. As a result, we reveal regions of model configuration space with an increased performance at a mild efficiency cost. We can roughly divide the hybrid model configuration space in the following 4 blocks:.

Capabilities of language models are known to come mainly from the training data, and that stays true for Falcon-H1 series. Besides the raw data prepared for the model, it is crucial how and when this data is shown during training. One such data strategy is commonly called curriculum learning, where simpler data is shown at the beginning of the training while the samples requiring more advanced reasoning are left for the end. Surprisingly, a completely opposite strategy worked best for us. Giving even the most complicated data, an advanced math problem or a long context sample, from the beginning of the training seems to give the model more time to learn features essential for handling the respective complex tasks.

Another key aspect is the scarcity of high-quality data. A common concern when training large models is brute force memorization of the data as opposed to its real understanding. To minimize the risk of such memorization, a common practice is not reusing data samples during training, or doing it at most a few times for the highest quality samples. A by-product of this strategy is data mixture being dominated by web samples that have disproportionally large volume compared to high-quality sources. We have found that the memorization effect might be a bit overestimated, and carefully estimating model's memorization window allows to reuse high-quality samples more often without any harm to model's generalization ability.

Classical μP is a technique heavily rooted in theory of neural networks but with a clear practical application: if one finds optimal training hyperparameters at a single base model size, it can be effortlessly transferred to other, typically bigger, model sizes using Mup scaling rules. We employed Mup hyperparameter transfer for the whole Falcon-H1 series, greatly reducing experimentation time and making it possible to train 6 models in parallel.

It has been revealed that on top of that, we made the next step into inner workings behind μP to further boost the model performance. In a nutshell, each component of the model “wants” to train at its own intensity, and that intensity depends on the size of the component. μP scaling rules take into account this dependence through so-called ``μP multipliers'' to enable optimal hyperparameter transfer. However, classical μP uses trivial multipliers of 1 at the base model size, which corresponds to a nasusmption that intensity of all components are already optimal at the base size. We discard this assumption and tune the multipliers at the base model size. Specifically, we have divided model parameters into 35 fine-grained groups and performed a joint optimization of the respective 35 multipliers.

Recent findings suggest that one of our first steps in working on Falcon-H1 series was treating and removing spikes that are known to be a serious issue for SSM-based models. The solution that has worked the best for us is placing dampening μP multipliers at a certain location of the SSM block. In addition to the smooth final model training, the removal of spikes is essential to get clean signals in the subsequent experiments.

Recent findings suggest that we have observed that many aspects of the training dynamics are linked together under a common theme of noise interpretation and control. This includes learning rate and batch size schedules, scaling of the learning rate with batch size, and the behavior of parameter norms. In particular, we have found the parameter norms to be mostly determined by the training hyperparameters rather than the model fitting the data. To take this into account, we have included weight decay, a hyperparameter that primarily controls parameter norms, into both the training schedule and μP multipliers.

The current Falcon-H1 models were trained without reasoning-specific fine-tuning, yet they already demonstrate strong general instruction-following capabilities. To highlight their performance, we present a detailed comparison of Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct against other top-performing Transformer models of similar or larger scales, including: Qwen3-32B (non-thinking mode), Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, Gemma3-27B, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E (109B) and LLaMA3.3-70B. For full evaluation settings and methodology, please refer to the Falcon-H1 GitHub page.

One of the standout features of the Falcon-H1 series is the strong performance of its compact models. Below, we compare 1.5B-scale instruct models. Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep-Instruct clearly outperforms leading models in its class, such as Qwen3-1.7B-Instruct. Even more notably, it performs on par with—or better than many 7B models, including Falcon3-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

🔎 Note: Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep and Falcon-H1-1.5B were trained using identical settings; the only difference lies in their architectural depth and width.

To give a picture of Falcon-H1 performance across languages, we provide average between Hellaswag and MMLU scores for 30B scale models and for a set of selected languages, including Arabic, German, Spanish, French, Hindi, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, and Swedish. It also demonstrates on-par performance in the other supported languages.

One of the standout features of Falcon-H1 is its ability to handle long-context inputs, an area where State Space Models (SSMs) offer significant advantages in terms of memory efficiency and computational cost.

Sources indicate that to demonstrate these capabilities, we evaluate Falcon-H1-34B-Instruct against Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct across a set of long-context benchmarks. We focus on three core task categories drawn from the Helmet benchmark suite - Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Natural Questions, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA; Recall tasks: JSON KV, RULER MK Needle, RULER MK UUID, RULER MV; Long Document QA tasks: ∞BENCH QA, ∞BENCH MC. These evaluations highlight Falcon-H1’s strength in scaling to longer sequences while maintaining high performance and efficiency.

According to recent reports, in addition, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation of the Falcon-H1 series alongside leading Transformer-based models across 23 benchmarks, covering multiple domains and model scales. You can explore the interactive results below—simply select the benchmarks most relevant to your use case to view the corresponding aggregated performance scores (below is a screenshort of our interactive plot in the official blogpost).

We provide a detailed comparison of Falcon-H1-34B-Base with other leading base models at the same or larger scale, including Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E (109B) and Gemma3-27B.

🔎 Note: Qwen3-32B does not at the moment offer a base model checkpoint.

Recent findings suggest that below, we compare 1.5B-scale base models. Falcon-H1-1.5B-Deep-Base clearly outperforms leading models in its class, such as Qwen3-1.7B-Base. Notably, it performs on par with Falcon3-7B, and even exceeds it on math and reasoning tasks, making it an excellent foundation for building small-scale reasoning-focused models.

For the base models, we also provide an interactive plot in our official blogpost showcasing their performance across 14 benchmarks, spanning multiple domains and various model scales (below is a screenshort of our interactive plot in the official blogpost).

In a recent development, we compare input (prefill) and output (generation) throughput between Falcon-H1 and Qwen2.5-32B in the plots below. While Transformers are slightly faster at shorter context lengths, our hybrid model becomes significantly more efficient as the context grows—achieving up to 4× speedup in input throughput and 8× in output throughput at longer sequence lengths. Benchmarks were run using our Falcon-H1 vLLM implementation and the official vLLM implementation of Qwen2.5-32B.

In a recent development, this performance gain highlights the scalability of the Falcon-H1 architecture. We attribute the throughput gap at small context lengths to the more mature optimizations of attention mechanisms, compared to current State Space Models (SSMs) implementations, in current inference pipelines.

⚙️ We invite the community to contribute to further optimizing SSM implementations — a promising direction for advancing the next generation of efficient LLMs.

Sources indicate that 🔎 Note: Input throughput measures how fast models process tokens when reading/encoding text. Output throughput measures how fast they generate upcoming tokens. The ratio line shows Falcon-H1/Qwen2.5 performance comparison.

Industry observers note that in line with our mission to foster AI accessibility and collaboration, Falcon-H1 is released under the Falcon LLM license. We hope the AI community finds these models valuable for research, application development, and further experimentation. Falcon-H1 is a continuation of our efforts to create more capable and efficient foundation models. We welcome feedback and collaboration from the community as we continue to refine and advance the capabilities of these models.

#81153. Industry News: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1531 w)

Industry News: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles.
  • But position and time are different.
  • In a recent development, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

In a recent development, the discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds.

Recent findings suggest that understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.

Industry observers note that however, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.

At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.

According to recent reports, tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.

It has been revealed that to appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.

Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.

Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling.

Recent findings suggest that to observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.

Recent findings suggest that in the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.

The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.

Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond.".

This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.

According to recent reports, what makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.

This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.

"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.

A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay.

Industry observers note that to understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit.".

Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.

At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.

For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit.".

The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.

The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.

A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time.

Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially.".

Recent findings suggest that in other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.

To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.

This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.

Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.

The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.

Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?

Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.

One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.

Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.

Such extreme conditions could give scientists latest ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.

Industry observers note that "In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.

The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.

"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the presently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.

That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.

For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.

Breaking: Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • In a recent development, unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • Industry observers note that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

In a recent development, unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a newly introduced form of computer memory.

Industry observers note that by harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," notes Yiwen Chu.

Sources indicate that the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

In a recent development, the researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an key role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are at the moment beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Recent findings suggest that many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

It has been revealed that another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

Upcoming Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

Recent findings suggest that the research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

Industry observers note that the achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

Sources indicate that to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

According to recent reports, "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

According to recent reports, successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments highlighted that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

According to recent reports, one of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Industry observers note that chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Recent findings suggest that practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising newly introduced route toward making those machines a reality.

Tiny Agents in Python: a MCP-powered agent in ~70 lines of code

📅 23 May 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that LATEST: tiny-agents now supports AGENTS.md standard.
  • Inspired by Tiny Agents in JS, we ported the idea to Python 🐍 and extended the huggingface_hub client SDK to act as a MCP Client so it can pull tools from MCP servers and pass them to the LLM during inference.
  • Recent findings suggest that MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes how Large Language Models (LLMs) interact with external tools and APIs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that LATEST: tiny-agents now supports AGENTS.md standard. 🥳.

Inspired by Tiny Agents in JS, we ported the idea to Python 🐍 and extended the huggingface_hub client SDK to act as a MCP Client so it can pull tools from MCP servers and pass them to the LLM during inference.

Recent findings suggest that MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes how Large Language Models (LLMs) interact with external tools and APIs. Essentially, it removed the need to write custom integrations for each tool, making it simpler to plug newly introduced capabilities into your LLMs.

Industry observers note that in this blog post, we'll show you how to get started with a tiny Agent in Python connected to MCP servers to unlock powerful tool capabilities. You'll see just how easy it is to spin up your own Agent and start building!

Spoiler : An Agent is essentially a while loop built right on top of an MCP Client!

This section walks you through how to use existing Tiny Agents. We'll cover the setup and the commands to get an agent running.

First, you need to install the latest version of huggingface_hub with the mcp extra to get all the necessary components.

Now, let's run an agent using the CLI!

The coolest part is that you can load agents directly from the Hugging Face Hub tiny-agents Dataset, or specify a path to your own local agent configuration!

If you don't provide a path to a specific agent configuration, our Tiny Agent will connect by default to the following two MCP servers:.

According to recent reports, the following example shows a web-browsing agent configured to use the Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and it comes equipped with a playwright MCP server, which lets it use a web browser! The agent config is loaded specifying its path in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents Hugging Face dataset.

When you run the agent, you'll see it load, listing the tools it has discovered from its connected MCP servers. Then, it's ready for your prompts!

do a Web Search for HF inference providers on Brave Search and open the first result and then give me the list of the inference providers supported on Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that you can also use Gradio Spaces as MCP servers! The following example uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and connects to a FLUX.1 [schnell] image generation HF Space as an MCP server. The agent is loaded from its configuration in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents dataset on the Hugging Face Hub.

Generate a 1024x1024 image of a tiny astronaut hatching from an egg on the surface of the moon.

Now that you've seen how to run existing Tiny Agents, the following sections will dive deeper into how they work and how to build your own.

It has been revealed that each agent's behavior (its default model, inference provider, which MCP servers to connect to, and its initial system prompt) is defined by an agent.json file. You can also provide a custom PROMPT.md in the same directory for a more detailed system prompt. Here is an example:.

Sources indicate that agent.json The model and provider fields specify the LLM and inference provider used by the agent. The servers array defines the MCP servers the agent will connect to. In this example, a "stdio" MCP server is configured. This type of server runs as a local process. The Agent starts it using the specified command and args, and then communicates with it via stdin/stdout to discover and execute available tools.

You can find more details about Hugging Face Inference Providers here.

Modern LLMs are built for function calling (or tool use), which enables people to easily build applications tailored to specific use cases and real-world tasks.

In a recent development, A function is defined by its schema, which informs the LLM what it does and what input arguments it expects. The LLM decides when to use a tool, the Agent then orchestrates running the tool and feeding the result back.

InferenceClient implements the same tool calling interface as the OpenAI Chat Completions API, which is the established standard for inference providers and the community.

It has been revealed that the MCPClient is the heart of our tool-use functionality. It's now part of huggingface_hub and uses the AsyncInferenceClient to communicate with LLMs.

The full MCPClient code is in here if you want to follow along using the actual code 🤓.

Key responsibilities of the MCPClient:.

​​Here’s a glimpse of how it connects to an MCP server (the add_mcp_server method):.

Recent findings suggest that it supports stdio servers for local tools (like accessing your file system), and http servers for remote tools! It's also compatible with sse, which is the previous standard for remote tools.

The MCPClient's process_single_turn_with_tools method is where the LLM interaction happens. It sends the conversation history and available tools to the LLM via AsyncInferenceClient.chat.completions.create(..., stream=True).

First, the method determines all tools the LLM should be aware of for the current turn – this includes tools from MCP servers and any special "exit loop" tools for agent control; then, it makes a streaming call to the LLM:.

Industry observers note that as chunks arrive from the LLM, the method iterates through them. Each chunk is immediately yielded, then we reconstruct the complete text response and any tool calls.

Once the stream is complete, if the LLM requested any tool calls (now fully reconstructed in final_tool_calls), the method processes each one:.

It first checks if the tool called exits the loop (exit_loop_tool). If not, it finds the correct MCP session responsible for that tool and calls session.call_tool(). The result (or error response) is then formatted, added to the conversation history, and yielded so the Agent is aware of the tool's output.

With the MCPClient doing all the job for tool interactions, our Agent class becomes wonderfully simple. It inherits from MCPClient and adds the conversation management logic.

The Agent class is tiny and focuses on the conversational loop, the code can be found here.

It has been revealed that when an Agent is created, it takes an agent config (model, provider, which MCP servers to use, system prompt) and initializes the conversation history with the system prompt. The load_tools() method then iterates through the server configurations (defined in agent.json) and calls add_mcp_server (from the parent MCPClient) for each one, populating the agent's toolbox.

Industry observers note that the Agent.run() method is an asynchronous generator that processes a single user input. It manages the conversation turns, deciding when the agent's current task is complete.

There are a lot of cool ways to explore and expand upon the MCP Client and the Tiny Agent 🔥 Here are some ideas to get you started:.

Industry observers note that pull requests and contributions are welcome! Again, everything here is open source! 💎❤️.
