Breaking: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • According to recent reports, the approach has already revealed newly introduced candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • According to recent reports, one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

According to recent reports, the approach has already revealed newly introduced candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

It has been revealed that finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

Industry observers note that by "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez said. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

In a recent development, the new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Fresh Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Light plays an key role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

The newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

According to recent reports, these differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying new candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

Recent findings suggest that the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Sources indicate that martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

In a recent development, "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he remarked. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a front-end bug hiding in plain sight. It’s also a good illustration of where AI fits into front-end development. A prompt can describe what a component should look like and what should happen on click. The implementation still has to account for how people reach that control, activate it, and understand what changed.

Imagine asking an AI coding assistant for this:.

Build a React product carousel with previous and next arrows. Show one product at a time and wrap around at the ends.

Here’s an illustrative excerpt from the sort of implementation that can satisfy a quick mouse-driven demo:.

With some CSS, this can look exactly like the arrow in the design. The click handler advances the slide. A screenshot highlights the right layout.

Recent findings suggest that but a plain div sits outside the normal Tab sequence and has no native button semantics or keyboard activation. Adding tabIndex={0} would make it reachable while leaving Enter and Space behavior to be implemented separately. The browser already provides those behaviors through a native button.

Industry observers note that the real omission was in the requirement. “Show arrows” described the visual design. “Let someone reach and operate both controls with a keyboard” describes behavior you can test.

In a recent development, here’s a small version of the same carousel. The product data is fixed for the example, and the slides change only when the user requests it.

According to recent reports, the buttons have visible labels and work with both Enter and Space. When a slide changes, focus stays on the button you pressed, so you can press it again to keep browsing. The status message gives assistive technology a way to announce the fresh product and its position. Only the current product link is rendered, so Tab never lands on a link from a hidden slide.

According to recent reports, those are deliberate interaction choices. W3C’s carousel pattern provides guidance on using native buttons, keeping focus on the slide controls after activation, and handling automatic rotation when a design requires it. W3C Carousel Pattern.

I’d revise the original prompt like this:.

Build a manual React product carousel. Use native Previous and Next buttons. Both must work with Tab, Enter, and Space. Keep focus on the activated button after a slide change. Announce the new product name and position through a status message. Keep only the current product link in the Tab sequence. Show what happens when the user advances past the last product.

Industry observers note that the extra detail also gives you a review initiative. For this carousel, I’d use four checks:.

AI can help draft automated tests for the active link and wraparound behavior. I’d still run the keyboard and screen reader checks on the integrated page. A global stylesheet can erase a visible focus outline. A surrounding component can introduce an extra tab stop. The experience depends on the page the customer actually uses.

A checkout form can look complete with sample data and lose the customer’s entries when a request fails. A responsive header can match the design at two widths and overlap when a translated label is longer. A component can render correctly in isolation and shift the page when a slow image loads.

In a recent development, each example gives AI a concrete job. Ask it to preserve form values after a failed request, check the header with longer labels, or reserve space for the image. Then reproduce the condition yourself. Knowing which conditions matter is part of knowing the front end.

Recent findings suggest that the next time AI gives you a carousel that looks ready, start the review with your hands off the mouse. Tab to Next, press Space twice, and see where focus lands. That short test gives you evidence about how the component works for someone who relies on a keyboard.

AnythingLLM makes it easy to build powerful agentic assistants connecting to multiple MCP servers so you can connect your internal systems or even external services. Coupled with PC fleet management systems like Microsoft Intune, it’s a complete solution for IT organizations to enable employees with on-device AI capabilities.

Your best people are training your AI. Pay them for it

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • Early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills.
  • It has been revealed that when we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that early this year, we let every employee at ClickUp build their own AI agents and skills. Within months, we were running five agents for every employee, which felt like a transformation until we looked at the actual output and efficiency. In my own finance org, only 30% of employee-built agents and skills actually moved the needle. When we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern. The successful agents were created by employees who understood where a process in their work typically tends to break, and could turn that knowledge into clear rules and processes for artificial intelligence. We went from treating AI skill-building as an open invitation and instead focused on the people who were building AI agents that moved the needle. That fixed the quality problem, but handed us a harder problem to solve. When you take your best talent’s craft and turn it into an AI agent, what does that employee get in return for their expertise and labor? As more companies have the best employees train their AI, leaders must have a response to this question. Define the bar, then pay against it When we changed our AI skill-building process, eligibility depended on a manager’s recommendation and a strong performance review. But identifying the right people is half the work. Companies also need to establish what qualifies as a high-value skill, and what it is worth, before anyone starts building one. We created a framework that categorizes skills, assigns value, and determines the reward. It’s simple but makes it clear what employees should aim for and gives us a consistent way to reward them. At ClickUp, every skill falls into one of four categories, and each category has its own measure of success. One, revenue acceleration skills are measured by the pipeline or bookings they add, and two, cost elimination skills are measured by the spend they remove, like canceling a software we no longer use. Time compression skills, three, are measured by how much faster a core process runs, like closing the books or responding to a customer. And executive bounties, four, are specific problems our leadership team has identified, each with a reward attached. The category tells employees what type of skills to build with AI, but the proof of impact is what determines how much the AI skill is worth. Before creating a fresh AI skill, employees must record where the measure stands today, like how many sales meetings aren’t rebooked each month or how long it takes to close the books. Then they can build, and once the AI skill has been running long enough to show a consistent pattern of value, finance compares the new numbers against the starting point. Finance then subtracts the cost of running the AI skill, including tools and maintenance, and what remains is the value the employee created. We then look at what we would have paid to get the same result a different way. Hiring even a few experienced sellers is a major expense, so when one person’s AI skills deliver that same capacity, a standard raise no longer reflects what their work is worth to the business. To determine the reward, we also consider how long the value will last. A skill that solves a single, contained problem earns a bonus. A skill or system the employee will keep running and improving earns a permanent raise, since the company will keep benefiting from that work every year. Together, these steps give us a dollar amount for each AI skill created, which we can use to determine the compensation ranging from a one-time bonus to becoming part of our “unicorn” group. Unicorns are employees whose AI work changes what an entire team can do, and they receive a merit increase of more than 30% along with eligibility for compensation up to $1 million at the top of the band. For example, one growth operations manager identified 17 places where we were regularly losing potential sales and built 11 AI skills to address them. Those skills recovered hundreds of thousands of dollars in pipeline and increased the number of sales prospects by 25%. They also saved every sales rep about 90 minutes in their day, which is equivalent to seven sellers’ worth of capacity. Because the results were large, verified, and directly tied to revenue, this employee joined our “unicorn” group. Reward your talent for making their expertise reusable Your best people are already training your AI. They are handing over the part of themselves that made them hard to replace, and the company can keep using that knowledge long after they have moved on. Hoarding what only one person knows feels like job security, but it is ultimately a ceiling. The people thriving in this model build the skill, hand over their knowledge, and move to the next problem. Each handoff allows them to take on a bigger, more interesting challenge. This is the model companies should build toward as AI moves deeper into knowledge work—rewarding people for making their expertise reusable. That judgment is intellectual property, and paying for it is how you build AI that works while retaining top talent.

It has been revealed that when we looked into which AIs brought the most value, there was an obvious pattern. The successful agents were created by employees who understood where a process in their work typically tends to break, and could turn that knowledge into clear rules and processes for artificial intelligence.

We went from treating AI skill-building as an open invitation and instead focused on the people who were building AI agents that moved the needle.

Recent findings suggest that that fixed the quality problem, but handed us a harder problem to solve. When you take your best talent’s craft and turn it into an AI agent, what does that employee get in return for their expertise and labor? As more companies have the best employees train their AI, leaders must have a response to this question.

When we changed our AI skill-building process, eligibility depended on a manager’s recommendation and a strong performance review. But identifying the right people is half the work. Companies also need to establish what qualifies as a high-value skill, and what it is worth, before anyone starts building one.

Sources indicate that we created a framework that categorizes skills, assigns value, and determines the reward. It’s simple but makes it clear what employees should aim for and gives us a consistent way to reward them.

Recent findings suggest that at ClickUp, every skill falls into one of four categories, and each category has its own measure of success. One, revenue acceleration skills are measured by the pipeline or bookings they add, and two, cost elimination skills are measured by the spend they remove, like canceling a software we no longer use. Time compression skills, three, are measured by how much faster a core process runs, like closing the books or responding to a customer. And executive bounties, four, are specific problems our leadership team has identified, each with a reward attached.

Sources indicate that the category tells employees what type of skills to build with AI, but the proof of impact is what determines how much the AI skill is worth. Before creating a new AI skill, employees must record where the measure stands today, like how many sales meetings aren’t rebooked each month or how long it takes to close the books.

Then they can build, and once the AI skill has been running long enough to show a consistent pattern of value, finance compares the newly introduced numbers against the starting point. Finance then subtracts the cost of running the AI skill, including tools and maintenance, and what remains is the value the employee created.

According to recent reports, we then look at what we would have paid to get the same result a different way. Hiring even a few experienced sellers is a major expense, so when one person’s AI skills deliver that same capacity, a standard raise no longer reflects what their work is worth to the business.

Industry observers note that to determine the reward, we also consider how long the value will last. A skill that solves a single, contained problem earns a bonus. A skill or system the employee will keep running and improving earns a permanent raise, since the company will keep benefiting from that work every year.

Industry observers note that together, these steps give us a dollar amount for each AI skill created, which we can use to determine the compensation ranging from a one-time bonus to becoming part of our “unicorn” group. Unicorns are employees whose AI work changes what an entire team can do, and they receive a merit increase of more than 30% along with eligibility for compensation up to $1 million at the top of the band.

For example, one growth operations manager identified 17 places where we were regularly losing potential sales and built 11 AI skills to address them. Those skills recovered hundreds of thousands of dollars in pipeline and increased the number of sales prospects by 25%. They also saved every sales rep about 90 minutes in their day, which is equivalent to seven sellers’ worth of capacity. Because the results were large, verified, and directly tied to revenue, this employee joined our “unicorn” group.

Your best people are already training your AI. They are handing over the part of themselves that made them hard to replace, and the company can keep using that knowledge long after they have moved on. Hoarding what only one person knows feels like job security, but it is ultimately a ceiling. The people thriving in this model build the skill, hand over their knowledge, and move to the next problem. Each handoff allows them to take on a bigger, more interesting challenge.

Recent findings suggest that this is the model companies should build toward as AI moves deeper into knowledge work—rewarding people for making their expertise reusable. That judgment is intellectual property, and paying for it is how you build AI that works while retaining top talent.

🐯 Liger GRPO meets TRL

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning.
  • In a recent development, however, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, TL; DR Liger supercharges TRL’s Group Relative Policy Optimization GRPO Trainer by slashing memory usage by 40% with zero drop in model quality. We also added support for FSDP and PEFT, making it easier than ever to scale GRPO across multiple GPUs.

It has been revealed that fine-tuning language models using reinforcement learning (RL) is a crucial step in a model's training lifecycle for steering models towards desirable behaviours which are more complex than can be achieved through typical supervised fine-tuning. RL has traditionally been applied to optimize large language models (LLMs) using the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm. This approach, often associated with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), utilizes a separately trained reward model to guide the fine-tuning of the primary model.

In a recent development, however, RLHF with PPO is a very resource-hungry approach - PPO requires loading multiple models in memory (policy, value, reward, and reference models), and also requires several iterations of fine-tuning reward and base models to achieve the desired results. The success of RLHF also depends on the capability of the reward model to effectively discriminate between desired and un-desired behaviour from our model.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has seen significant recent popularity alongside DeepSeek's R1 model. GRPO eschews the pre-trained reward model and value models used in RLHF and instead relies on verifiable reward functions which can check the correctness of a model's output in a closed-form manner without needing an external reward model. This has resulted in massive improvements when using GRPO instead of PPO for fine-tuning on domains which are easily verifiable, such as teaching a model to reason, and perform well on math and coding tasks.

The following diagram highlights the GRPO vs PPO training pipeline (ref: Figure 4 of DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models):.

Sources indicate that that said, RL training still eats up a ton of GPU memory, so there's still plenty of room for optimizations here. In this blog post, we talk about an optimization that we recently added to TRL that cuts peak memory usage by 40% during GRPO Training, and we also dive into how to scale GRPO to multiple GPUs and nodes without losing performance or correctness.

We extended the Liger Chunked Loss approach to the GRPO Loss, which lets us avoid having to store the full logits in memory for every training step. The calculation of logits, which involves the model's output head, is a significant contributor to peak memory usage, especially when dealing with large vocabularies, long sequence lengths, or large batch sizes. We address this by chunking the input to the lm_head across the batch and running the forward pass one chunk at a time.

Recent findings suggest that but if you just implement it in a straightforward way, you won't actually be able to reduce the peak memory since you'd still need to keep all the logits in GPU memory for the backward pass. To get around that, we calculate the gradients for each loss chunk (with respect to the input chunk and the lm_head weight) during the forward pass, and then accumulate them as we go through each chunk.

Here's the visualization of the optimization (ref: Byron Hsu):.

We recently integrated Liger GRPO with TRL in PR #3184, so now you can use the Liger GRPO loss just by setting use_liger_loss to True in your GRPOConfig and enjoy the memory savings!

Heads up: these features aren't in the latest TRL release yet, so you'll need to install TRL from source for now:.

and then you can use it like this:.

Industry observers note that we ran a bunch of GRPO experiments with and without the Liger GRPO Loss to see how things compare. For the policy model, we used Qwen3-0.6B and played around with different batch sizes. All the experiments were run on the gsm8k dataset using its reward functions.

Here's the plots of peak memory usage vs batch size for both FP32 and BF16 training. As expected, the memory savings get better with larger batch sizes since we chunk along the batch dimension. So when the batch size goes up, the Liger chunked loss ends up using a lot less memory, up to 40% less, compared to the regular (non-liger) version.

Industry observers note that quick note: Right now, we only support FP32, but we're working on open-sourcing BF16 support for Liger GRPO in TRL. The BF16 results shown here are from internal patches we've been testing.

Recent findings suggest that we also show that Liger Loss is effectively accurate. As seen in the plot, rewards over training steps stay pretty much the same as what you'd see using the standard TRL implementation.

We also added FSDP and PEFT support to Liger GRPO Loss in PR #3260 and PR #3355, respectively, allowing users to easily scale their experiments across multiple GPUs or nodes. PEFT techniques such as LoRA and QLoRA reduce the number of trainable parameters by only tuning the weights of smaller adapter weights on top of the original model, significantly lowering memory pressure as gradients, activations, and optimizer states for the entire model don't need to be held in memory. Additionally, using PEFT in GRPO allows one to forgo loading a separate reference model during training, as we can obtain the original, unmodified model during training by simply disabling the LoRA adapters.

Here, we show a multi-GPU GRPO training plot using FSDP and PEFT, where we compare the maximum training batch size possible with and without the Liger Loss across different Qwen3 model sizes. We found that with Liger, we were able to bump up the batch size by around 1.5 to 1.8x!

Industry observers note that to accelerate text generation during training, Liger Loss can be effectively combined with TRL's integrated vLLM server. This significantly speeds up the collection of rollout data with minimal overhead and offers a seamless integration experience.

Sources indicate that start the vLLM Server: First, launch the vLLM server. This server will handle the generation requests from your training script. Open a terminal and run:.

Note: We assign CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 to run the vLLM server on a specific GPU (GPU 1 in this case), leaving other GPUs free for training.

Configure and Run Your Training Script: Next, modify your training script to use the vLLM server. The key change is setting use_vllm=True in your GRPOConfig.

Sources indicate that launch the Training: Finally, run your training script using accelerate launch (or python if not using Accelerate for multi-GPU/distributed training). Make sure to target a different GPU for training if your vLLM server is occupying one.

(Assuming your script is named train.py and you want to run training on GPU 0).

By following these steps, you can leverage vLLM for faster generation turnarounds during your GRPO training with Liger Loss.

According to recent reports, with the integration of Liger-GRPO into TRL, alongside FSDP and PEFT support, fine-tuning language models with GRPO is now more memory-efficient and scalable than ever. We encourage the community to try out these fresh features and share their feedback to help us further improve RL training for LLMs.

it depends on the setup usually, might be effective in boost, and may not either!

In our experiments, we observed no significant difference in training speeds with and without liger.

4 phases of becoming a great leader

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his new book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World.
  • Below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his fresh book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World.
  • Martignetti is a leadership and workplace culture adviser, global keynote speaker, experience designer, and the host of The Virtual Campfire podcast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his new book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World. Martignetti is a leadership and workplace culture adviser, global keynote speaker, experience designer, and the host of The Virtual Campfire podcast. He began his career as a finance and strategy executive in the high-tech and life sciences industries before leaving the corporate world to help leaders integrate all of who they are into how they lead. What’s the Big Idea? The world does not need more exhausted leaders. It needs integrated and multidimensional leaders who can serve as lighthouses for others. If you are ready to stop fragmenting your brilliance and start illuminating it, then the four phases of Illuminating Hidden Brilliance are for you. Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Martignetti himself—in the Next Big Idea app, or buy the book. 1. Discover The first phase is about uncovering what’s been hidden. For decades, we’ve been sold a seductive story: focus narrowly, pick a lane, master one thing, and leave the rest of yourself at the door. That story made sense in the age of the assembly line, when problems were linear and predictable. That isn’t the world we’re leading in now. I lived this myself. Early in my career, I took pride in being “the numbers guy.” But my real breakthroughs never came from the spreadsheets alone. They came when I paired that analytical rigor with something more creative, like sketching visual maps or drawing metaphors that helped executives feel the strategy instead of just understand it. Now that AI has arrived, it could run those same models in seconds. But it is only able to replace the mechanical part of my contributions. What made me valuable was never the calculations. It was the ability to connect analysis with narrative and logic with imagination. Integration isn’t dilution; it’s differentiation. AI is the ultimate specialist. Our human edge is curiosity, empathy, intuition, creativity, and the ability to make meaning across boundaries. So how do you find what’s been hidden? One way is what I call Flashpoint Excavation. When I began interviewing guests on my podcast, I noticed a pattern. Every leader, whether a CEO, an artist, or a change maker, could trace their most significant growth to a single inflection point: a moment when the old story stopped working and a new one began. Those moments often came disguised as endings. But each one carried an ember of brilliance. When have you hidden a part of yourself to fit the mold of professional success? And what did it cost you? 2. Distill Not every dimension needs equal airtime. Distilling is about deciding what matters most, what wants expression now, and what deserves protection. The heart of this phase is learning to navigate polarities. Being multidimensional means living in constant tension: focus and freedom, logic and intuition, ambition and rest. We’re taught to pick a side and eliminate complexity. But these tensions aren’t flaws to fix. They’re the forces that shape growth. I once coached a healthcare executive who constantly wrestled with the tension between compassion and performance. When we mapped that polarity, she realized her empathy wasn’t softening her results. It was strengthening her influence. Her teams trusted her more deeply, which made accountability easier to sustain. When she stopped choosing between results and relationships, both grew stronger. I think of it like jazz. There’s a structure, a key, a beat, and within it, there’s improvisation. The music works because of the relationship between discipline and play. Leadership works the same way. One of my clients, Alina, keeps a simple note on her desk that reads, “Hold both ambition and humility lightly.” Whenever she feels herself slipping into all-or-nothing thinking, those words bring her back. Distilling also means finding your edge. When I left the corporate world, I thought freedom would be the reward. Instead, I found the chaos of too many possibilities. One morning, after weeks of trying to design the perfect business initiative, I closed my laptop, walked outside, and said to myself, “I don’t need more space. I need better focus.” So, I ran a small experiment. I called it Campfire Conversations: intimate gatherings where leaders shared the stories behind their breakthroughs. That single experiment created a depth I could never have planned, and it became the foundation of my work. I call this the Edge Effect. Brilliance doesn’t happen in endless open space. It happens at the edges, where freedom meets form. 3. Design With clarity in place, the third phase is about designing the practices, rhythms, and environments that sustain your brilliance. This is where leadership becomes intentional instead of reactive. The first quality to design for is elasticity: the capacity to bend without breaking. I love the story of Lego. In the early 2000s, the manufacturer was on the verge of collapse. It had expanded into video games, theme parks, fashion, and television. The problem wasn’t too little innovation. It was too much, too fast. When Jørgen Vig Knudstorp became CEO, he did two things that seemed contradictory. First, he set limits. He cut the number of unique pieces in half and guided every decision with one question: Does this build on the brick? Then he opened the doors wider than ever, inviting fans around the world to design new sets. Structure and imagination stopped being enemies and became dance partners. As he put it, “We needed to become smaller and bigger at the same time.” The second piece of Design is Presence Engineering. You cannot live in a multidimensional life with a one-dimensional operating system. Without intentional practices, expressing more of yourself can turn into scattered energy and role-switching fatigue. Presence Engineering gives you a through line that holds your whole identity, so you don’t lose yourself as you expand. When you design for integration, remarkable things can happen. Dina, a cardiac surgeon I once coached, told me privately, “I feel like a robot sometimes.” When I asked her the last time she’d lost herself in the moment, she quietly said, “When I used to paint.” She had hidden that part of herself for years. “You can’t be a serious surgeon and a painter,” she said. A few weeks later, she faced one of the most complex cases of her career. She stepped up to the table and saw the patient’s heart differently. “It looked like something I wanted to paint,” she told me. Her team later described her movement that day as fluid, and almost choreographed, and the surgery was a success. She designed small practices: sketching before difficult cases, taking two minutes outside before scrubbing in, and hanging her paintings in her office. Not only that, but she began telling her residents, “Technical precision saves lives, but your presence saves you.” 4. Deliver The final phase is about extending your integration outward into conversations, teams, organizations, and communities, so your leadership becomes a catalyst for collective brilliance. It often starts with a single conversation. I once worked with a global tech company that was six weeks from a major product launch, and every meeting felt like a battlefield. Engineering said the product wasn’t ready. Marketing said the messaging was unclear. Finance said the budget was already over. No one could see the whole picture. Then a quiet, mid-level product manager stepped in and said, “Before we talk about deliverables, let’s talk about realities. Paint me the picture of what you’re seeing.” Each group sketched its version of the problem on a whiteboard, and as they drew, a pattern appeared that everyone could finally see. Within two days, they’d redesigned the launch, and the product shipped on time. She didn’t solve their problems. What she did was build a bridge between their worlds. That’s the kind of leader the future needs: interpreters and bridge builders who design conversations where people feel seen. To sustain that impact over the long arc of a career, I come back to the image of a lighthouse. A lighthouse doesn’t shine in every direction with equal intensity. It doesn’t react to every wave passing. It stands rooted, and it rotates in a steady rhythm, and its light is focused, which is precisely why ships can steer by it. Think of Ernest Shackleton. In 1915, his ship, the Endurance, was trapped in Antarctic ice and eventually sank. He understood that the greatest danger to his crew was the slow erosion of hope. So he became their lighthouse, moving deliberately between roles: strategist, caretaker, challenger, and anchor, depending on what the moment required. His men later said they watched Shackleton more closely than the sun. Every single crew member survived. His brilliance wasn’t dramatic. It was disciplined. People rarely copy what leaders say. They copy who leaders are. When you model wholeness, you give others permission to bring theirs. The world doesn’t need more exhausted leaders shining endlessly in every direction. It requires integrated, multidimensional leaders who can shine steadily enough to guide others home. You don’t need to become louder, only clearer. And you don’t need to become someone new. You just need to let more of who you already are into the room. This article originally appeared in Next Big Idea Club magazine and is reprinted with permission. A few weeks later, she faced one of the most complex cases of her career. She stepped up to the table and saw the patient’s heart differently. “It looked like something I wanted to paint,” she told me. Her team later described her movement that day as fluid, and almost choreographed, and the surgery was a success.

She designed small practices: sketching before difficult cases, taking two minutes outside before scrubbing in, and hanging her paintings in her office. Not only that, but she began telling her residents, “Technical precision saves lives, but your presence saves you.”.

The final phase is about extending your integration outward into conversations, teams, organizations, and communities, so your leadership becomes a catalyst for collective brilliance. It often starts with a single conversation.

I once worked with a global tech manufacturer that was six weeks from a major product launch, and every meeting felt like a battlefield. Engineering said the product wasn’t ready. Marketing said the messaging was unclear. Finance said the budget was already over. No one could see the whole picture.

It has been revealed that then a quiet, mid-level product manager stepped in and noted, “Before we talk about deliverables, let’s talk about realities. Paint me the picture of what you’re seeing.” Each group sketched its version of the problem on a whiteboard, and as they drew, a pattern appeared that everyone could finally see. Within two days, they’d redesigned the launch, and the product shipped on time.

She didn’t solve their problems. What she did was build a bridge between their worlds. That’s the kind of leader the future needs: interpreters and bridge builders who design conversations where people feel seen.

To sustain that impact over the long arc of a career, I come back to the image of a lighthouse. A lighthouse doesn’t shine in every direction with equal intensity. It doesn’t react to every wave passing. It stands rooted, and it rotates in a steady rhythm, and its light is focused, which is precisely why ships can steer by it.

Think of Ernest Shackleton. In 1915, his ship, the Endurance, was trapped in Antarctic ice and eventually sank. He understood that the greatest danger to his crew was the slow erosion of hope. So he became their lighthouse, moving deliberately between roles: strategist, caretaker, challenger, and anchor, depending on what the moment required. His men later remarked they watched Shackleton more closely than the sun. Every single crew member survived.

His brilliance wasn’t dramatic. It was disciplined. People rarely copy what leaders say. They copy who leaders are. When you model wholeness, you give others permission to bring theirs.

The world doesn’t need more exhausted leaders shining endlessly in every direction. It requires integrated, multidimensional leaders who can shine steadily enough to guide others home. You don’t need to become louder, only clearer. And you don’t need to become someone latest. You just need to let more of who you already are into the room.

Sources indicate that ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

It has been revealed that in this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

In a recent development, an LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:.

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process claims "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

A few things make it worse in your app:.

According to recent reports, newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:.

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

Sources indicate that northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:.

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:.

Recent findings suggest that the traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:.

Every version calls the model through one small helper:.

According to recent reports, we're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

Recent findings suggest that opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply mentioned it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:.

Sources indicate that it treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:.

Sources indicate that northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

Recent findings suggest that the model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:.

Right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:.

Sources indicate that delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data notes nothing about price matching:.

It said it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

Sources indicate that if version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":.

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

According to recent reports, version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:.

Recent findings suggest that zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

Here's what it read from the 60L email:.

It has been revealed that the model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

Sources indicate that A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

If all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Sources indicate that second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:.

For the return email, that gives:.

Recent findings suggest that every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

Recent findings suggest that the last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

Third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:.

Recent findings suggest that it's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:.

In a recent development, if a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

It's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

It has been revealed that this script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:.

Sources indicate that the check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:.

Version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:.

In a recent development, no model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

It cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

In a recent development, not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

Industry observers note that collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:.

The model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.

#81137. Breaking: SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life

Breaking: SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues.
  • Recent findings suggest that in its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues.
  • It has been revealed that this sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues. But rarely has an SNL sketch resonated as deeply—and prompted as many national conversations—as the Sister commercial parody that aired on November 14, 2026. This sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents. The parody claims that simply texting the words “Dad fell” to your sister will prompt her to quit her job, break her lease, and completely upend her life to come take care of him—for free. Clearly, the all-male writing team of Streeter Seidell (who dedicated the sketch to his sister, Heidi), Mikey Day, Simon Rich, and Chase Rosenberg are onto something. AARP found that as of 2025, 59 million Americans were providing care for an adult loved one, and women made up 61% of those caregivers. And it’s taking a toll. AARP reports that caregivers of adults over 50 have been caregiving for 5 years and spend 26 hours per week providing care—up from an average of 3.9 years and 22 hours per week as of 2020. About 20% of those caregivers rate themselves as having fair or poor health, and they report an average of 7 poor mental health days per month. These unpaid caregivers spend an average of $11,508 per year on caretaking, which is equal to 31% of the median household income. Women across the country may have laughed through their rage at this painfully accurate comedy—but they deserve more than the mere satisfaction of simply feeling seen by an incisive satire. Cameron Huddleston, author of Mom and Dad, We Need to Talk, and Dr. Darla Bishop, financial wellness expert, public health researcher, and author of How to Afford Everything, offer the following practical suggestions for how America’s siblings can take care of aging parents without upending their lives, bankrupting themselves, or emptying their retirement accounts. Don’t minimize the costs of caregiving The humor of the SNL sketch relies on the family’s ignoring and downplaying the very real cost the sister pays when she becomes the caregiver. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “If you’re cutting back your hours, turning down promotions, or dipping into your retirement savings, caregiving has a price tag, even when no money changes hands.” But the sister faces more than just financial costs. We see her clash with her father and brother and argue with her husband. “In my work, I teach people to think about their three currencies: time, energy, and money,” Dr. Bishop notes. “Caregiving requires all three.” So rather than the sister being a free resource, as Mulaney claims in the ad, she’s using up all of her currencies while her brother pays nothing. Recognizing the heavy costs of caregiving is the first step to breaking the dynamic illustrated by SNL. “I want families to understand that just because you can afford to help your parents today doesn’t mean you can afford the long-term consequences of doing it alone,” Dr. Bishop says. Don’t ignore available resources “When a parent needs care, families assume they have two choices: do it themselves or pay someone else,” Dr. Bishop says. “But there are resources in between, and finding them could save your family thousands of dollars and countless hours.” Specifically, Dr. Bishop recommends starting with your local Area Agency on Aging, which can help you find services like transportation, meal delivery, respite care, and caregiver support. She also suggests exploring the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov to help find affordable caregiving near you. You also don’t have to figure out these services on your own. According to Huddleston, an aging life care professional can help. (These people were previously known as geriatric care managers.) “These professionals will be familiar with resources in your area—from adult day care centers to government programs and community assistance,” Huddleston says. To find an aging life care professional, check out the Aging Life Care Association in your area. And don’t forget other, potentially overlooked resources available to you. Your parents may be eligible for Medicaid, depending on their income, health, and location. The VA’s Aid and Attendance program provides benefits for veterans and their spouses that help cover the cost of assistance with activities of daily living. Even your own employer benefits may help. “Some workplaces offer caregiver support, flexible scheduling, or access to care coordinators,” Dr. Bishop says. Don’t go it alone Huddleston was a caregiver for her mom, who had Alzheimer’s disease. One of her regrets about that time was not asking for more help from her family. “If I had asked, I would’ve gotten more help,” she says, “but I didn’t want to be a burden on others.” This gets to a common mindset the SNL skit illustrates: A lot of women are afraid to ask for help. “We assume it’s our responsibility, and we don’t want to appear like we can’t manage that responsibility,” Huddleston says. While it’s true that sometimes women ask for help and don’t receive it, Huddleston believes that many families assume the caregiver has it covered. “My husband was great about helping with my mom, doing so much to support me and her,” she says. “I’d love to see more men respond that way. But if they’re not seeing the toll it takes on the caregiver, as my husband saw daily with me, they probably aren’t even aware of how much of a sacrifice it is to care for a parent.” When asking for help, Dr. Bishop’s three currencies framework can help you figure out who can do what. You can divide responsibilities based on the time, energy, and money you each bring to the table. “Maybe one sibling lives nearby and can take Mom to appointments while another has more financial flexibility and can contribute toward paid care,” Dr. Bishop suggests. “A third might be great at managing paperwork, coordinating benefits, or researching resources.” Huddleston recommends keeping a running list of the types of support you need so that you’re prepared to make specific requests. “You might ask your brother to find an aging life care professional and cover the cost, to line up a housekeeper or lawn maintenance for your parents’ house, to pay for grocery delivery, to come stay with your parent in the evenings or weekends to give you a break,” she says. She also wants caregivers to let go of any guilt they have about asking for specific help. “It would be easier if men stepped up without being asked to help,” she says. “But if you’re not getting the help you need, don’t feel bad about asking for it.” Don’t wait to make decisions It’s easy to put off thinking about Mom and Dad’s health. None of us like to consider our parents’ mortality, and the idea of losing independence can be terrifying to an aging parent. But it’s easier to make good decisions before Dad falls, when no one is panicked or stressed. That’s why both Huddleston and Dr. Bishop both recommend having a family meeting well before there’s a crisis. “Put everything on the table,” Dr. Bishop says. “Ask yourselves, ‘What does our parent need? What resources do they already have? What can each of us realistically contribute without jeopardizing our own financial security?’” If your family tends to avoid such conversations, Huddleston suggests using the SNL skit as a jumping-off point to start the conversation. Don’t neglect your own long-term care planning Another way to break the cycle of relying on women’s unpaid caregiving is by planning for our own future care needs—and much earlier than you might think. “By the time you’re 50 years old, you should be thinking about long-term care and how you could pay for professional care so that you don’t have to rely entirely on a family member for support,” Huddleston says. “At that age (and into your early 60s if you’re healthy), you can still qualify for long-term care insurance or a hybrid life insurance policy with long-term care benefits.” Dr. Bishop also recommends getting your affairs in order—and that doesn’t just mean having a will in place. “One of the greatest gifts you can give your adult children is not making them play detective during a family crisis,” she says. Specifically, your kids should know where to find your crucial documents, who manages your money, what insurance you have, and your wishes in the event that you can’t make medical or financial decisions for yourself. So funny it hurts It’s unlikely that Saturday Night Live expected its three-minute parody to trigger a national reckoning about women’s disproportionate caregiving burden. But it struck a nerve for a very good reason. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “women aren’t the backup proposal. We are THE PLAN.” But that doesn’t mean we’re stuck with this dynamic forever. We can end our reliance on women’s unpaid labor by recognizing the heavy time, energy, and money cost of caregiving; exploring all available resources; refusing to let one person handle all caregiving; making proactive decisions; and planning ahead for our own long-term care needs. “The answer isn’t for women to stop caring about their families,” Dr. Bishop says. “It’s for families to stop assuming that caring automatically equals sacrificing your career, your finances, or your own well-being.”.

Recent findings suggest that in its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues. But rarely has an SNL sketch resonated as deeply—and prompted as many national conversations—as the Sister commercial parody that aired on November 14, 2026.

It has been revealed that this sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents. The parody claims that simply texting the words “Dad fell” to your sister will prompt her to quit her job, break her lease, and completely upend her life to come take care of him—for free.

It has been revealed that clearly, the all-male writing team of Streeter Seidell (who dedicated the sketch to his sister, Heidi), Mikey Day, Simon Rich, and Chase Rosenberg are onto something. AARP found that as of 2025, 59 million Americans were providing care for an adult loved one, and women made up 61% of those caregivers. And it’s taking a toll.

According to recent reports, AARP reports that caregivers of adults over 50 have been caregiving for 5 years and spend 26 hours per week providing care—up from an average of 3.9 years and 22 hours per week as of 2020. About 20% of those caregivers rate themselves as having fair or poor health, and they report an average of 7 poor mental health days per month. These unpaid caregivers spend an average of $11,508 per year on caretaking, which is equal to 31% of the median household income.

Women across the country may have laughed through their rage at this painfully accurate comedy—but they deserve more than the mere satisfaction of simply feeling seen by an incisive satire.

It has been revealed that cameron Huddleston, author of Mom and Dad, We Need to Talk, and Dr. Darla Bishop, financial wellness expert, public health researcher, and author of How to Afford Everything, offer the following practical suggestions for how America’s siblings can take care of aging parents without upending their lives, bankrupting themselves, or emptying their retirement accounts.

In a recent development, the humor of the SNL sketch relies on the family’s ignoring and downplaying the very real cost the sister pays when she becomes the caregiver. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “If you’re cutting back your hours, turning down promotions, or dipping into your retirement savings, caregiving has a price tag, even when no money changes hands.”.

Industry observers note that but the sister faces more than just financial costs. We see her clash with her father and brother and argue with her husband. “In my work, I teach people to think about their three currencies: time, energy, and money,” Dr. Bishop says. “Caregiving requires all three.”.

Recent findings suggest that so rather than the sister being a free resource, as Mulaney claims in the ad, she’s using up all of her currencies while her brother pays nothing. Recognizing the heavy costs of caregiving is the first step to breaking the dynamic illustrated by SNL.

Recent findings suggest that “I want families to understand that just because you can afford to help your parents today doesn’t mean you can afford the long-term consequences of doing it alone,” Dr. Bishop claims.

“When a parent needs care, families assume they have two choices: do it themselves or pay someone else,” Dr. Bishop says. “But there are resources in between, and finding them could save your family thousands of dollars and countless hours.”.

Sources indicate that specifically, Dr. Bishop recommends starting with your local Area Agency on Aging, which can help you find services like transportation, meal delivery, respite care, and caregiver support. She also suggests exploring the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov to help find affordable caregiving near you.

You also don’t have to figure out these services on your own. According to Huddleston, an aging life care professional can help. (These people were previously known as geriatric care managers.).

Recent findings suggest that “These professionals will be familiar with resources in your area—from adult day care centers to government programs and community assistance,” Huddleston indicates. To find an aging life care professional, check out the Aging Life Care Association in your area.

It has been revealed that and don’t forget other, potentially overlooked resources available to you. Your parents may be eligible for Medicaid, depending on their income, health, and location. The VA’s Aid and Attendance program provides benefits for veterans and their spouses that help cover the cost of assistance with activities of daily living. Even your own employer benefits may help.

“Some workplaces offer caregiver support, flexible scheduling, or access to care coordinators,” Dr. Bishop notes.

According to recent reports, huddleston was a caregiver for her mom, who had Alzheimer’s disease. One of her regrets about that time was not asking for more help from her family.

Sources indicate that “If I had asked, I would’ve gotten more help,” she says, “but I didn’t want to be a burden on others.” This gets to a common mindset the SNL skit illustrates: A lot of women are afraid to ask for help. “We assume it’s our responsibility, and we don’t want to appear like we can’t manage that responsibility,” Huddleston says.

While it’s true that sometimes women ask for help and don’t receive it, Huddleston believes that many families assume the caregiver has it covered.

Sources indicate that “My husband was great about helping with my mom, doing so much to support me and her,” she indicates. “I’d love to see more men respond that way. But if they’re not seeing the toll it takes on the caregiver, as my husband saw daily with me, they probably aren’t even aware of how much of a sacrifice it is to care for a parent.”.

Industry observers note that when asking for help, Dr. Bishop’s three currencies framework can help you figure out who can do what. You can divide responsibilities based on the time, energy, and money you each bring to the table.

According to recent reports, “Maybe one sibling lives nearby and can take Mom to appointments while another has more financial flexibility and can contribute toward paid care,” Dr. Bishop suggests. “A third might be great at managing paperwork, coordinating benefits, or researching resources.”.

Industry observers note that huddleston recommends keeping a running list of the types of support you need so that you’re prepared to make specific requests. “You might ask your brother to find an aging life care professional and cover the cost, to line up a housekeeper or lawn maintenance for your parents’ house, to pay for grocery delivery, to come stay with your parent in the evenings or weekends to give you a break,” she says.

It has been revealed that she also wants caregivers to let go of any guilt they have about asking for specific help. “It would be easier if men stepped up without being asked to help,” she states. “But if you’re not getting the help you need, don’t feel bad about asking for it.”.

In a recent development, it’s easy to put off thinking about Mom and Dad’s health. None of us like to consider our parents’ mortality, and the idea of losing independence can be terrifying to an aging parent. But it’s easier to make good decisions before Dad falls, when no one is panicked or stressed. That’s why both Huddleston and Dr. Bishop both recommend having a family meeting well before there’s a crisis.

“Put everything on the table,” Dr. Bishop indicates. “Ask yourselves, ‘What does our parent need? What resources do they already have? What can each of us realistically contribute without jeopardizing our own financial security?’”.

If your family tends to avoid such conversations, Huddleston suggests using the SNL skit as a jumping-off point to start the conversation.

Another way to break the cycle of relying on women’s unpaid caregiving is by planning for our own future care needs—and much earlier than you might think.

“By the time you’re 50 years old, you should be thinking about long-term care and how you could pay for professional care so that you don’t have to rely entirely on a family member for support,” Huddleston notes. “At that age (and into your early 60s if you’re healthy), you can still qualify for long-term care insurance or a hybrid life insurance policy with long-term care benefits.”.

Sources indicate that dr. Bishop also recommends getting your affairs in order—and that doesn’t just mean having a will in place. “One of the greatest gifts you can give your adult children is not making them play detective during a family crisis,” she claims.

Specifically, your kids should know where to find your important documents, who manages your money, what insurance you have, and your wishes in the event that you can’t make medical or financial decisions for yourself.

It’s unlikely that Saturday Night Live expected its three-minute parody to trigger a national reckoning about women’s disproportionate caregiving burden. But it struck a nerve for a very good reason.

Recent findings suggest that as Dr. Bishop puts it, “women aren’t the backup blueprint. We are THE PLAN.”.

But that doesn’t mean we’re stuck with this dynamic forever. We can end our reliance on women’s unpaid labor by recognizing the heavy time, energy, and money cost of caregiving; exploring all available resources; refusing to let one person handle all caregiving; making proactive decisions; and planning ahead for our own long-term care needs.

“The answer isn’t for women to stop caring about their families,” Dr. Bishop states. “It’s for families to stop assuming that caring automatically equals sacrificing your career, your finances, or your own well-being.”.
