Sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers initiative around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

According to recent reports, actual development rarely follows that plan. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

Recent findings suggest that developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

Sources indicate that historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

Recent findings suggest that completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

Carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

Sources indicate that interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production issues. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing fresh features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

Recent findings suggest that capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

These records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual problem could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

Industry observers note that historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating latest tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

The first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

In a recent development, for example, suppose a team needs to estimate a fresh API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

Recent findings suggest that the average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the new estimate.

According to recent reports, however, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The newly introduced integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

As a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying glitch.

It has been revealed that research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

Start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100.

Suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

For example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

Avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

According to recent reports, A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

Consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

Sources indicate that the actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

Teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

Sources indicate that for example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

In a recent development, suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook important differences.

A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

It has been revealed that in such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

Sources indicate that however, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Industry observers note that historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

Reduce Scope After Repeated Overruns.

If several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Reserve Capacity for Unplanned Work.

According to recent reports, production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Adjust for Complexity and Dependencies.

Recent findings suggest that historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as important inputs to sprint forecasting.

Industry observers note that when you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

In a recent development, historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

In a recent development, however, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

TimeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

In a recent development, with this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them proposal similar work more accurately.

TimeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

In a recent development, however, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

According to recent reports, apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

Sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a proposal, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

In a recent development, ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

Not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Recent findings suggest that historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

Sources indicate that 1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

In a recent development, sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

In a recent development, velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning shows whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

Industry observers note that 2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

Recent findings suggest that bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

It has been revealed that these metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

In a recent development, **3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **.

Teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

It has been revealed that when data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

Sources indicate that 4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Time tracking data indicates how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Sources indicate that technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

In a recent development, hugging Face transformers library is the standard for working with state-of-the-art models — from experimenting with cutting-edge research to fine-tuning on custom data. Its simplicity, flexibility, and expansive model zoo make it a powerful tool for rapid development.

Recent findings suggest that but once you're ready to move from notebooks to production, inference performance becomes mission-critical. That’s where SGLang comes in.

According to recent reports, designed for high-throughput, low-latency inference, SGLang now offers seamless integration with transformers as a backend. This means you can pair the flexibility of transformers with the raw performance of SGLang.

Let’s dive into what this integration enables and how you can use it.

SGLang now supports Hugging Face transformers as a backend, letting you run any transformers-compatible model with high-performance inference out of the box.

No native support needed — SGLang automatically falls back to Transformers when needed, or you can set impl="transformers" explicitly.

Let’s walk through a simple text generation example with meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct to compare both approaches.

transformers library is great for experimentation, small-scale tasks and training, but it's not optimized for high-volume or low-latency scenarios.

In a recent development, SGLang takes a different track, prioritizing efficiency with features like RadixAttention (a memory-efficient attention mechanism). Inference with SGLang is noticeably faster and more resource-efficient, especially under load. Here’s the same task in SGlang using an offline engine:.

Or you can spin a server and send requests:.

Note that SGLang also offers an OpenAI-compatible API, making it a drop-in replacement for external services.

With the new transformers backend integration, SGLang can now automatically fall back to using transformers models it doesn’t natively support. This means in practice:.

This unlocks faster inference and optimized deployment (e.g enabling RadixAttention) without sacrificing the simplicity and versatility of transformers ecosystem.

It has been revealed that note that specifying the impl parameter is optional. If the model is not natively supported by SGLang, it switches to transformers implementation on its own.

According to recent reports, any model on the Hugging Face Hub that works with transformers using trust_remote_code=True and properly implements attention is compatible with SGLang. You can find the exact requirements in the official documentation. If your custom model meets these criteria, all you need to do is set trust_remote_code=True when loading it.

Industry observers note that kyutai Team’s Helium isn’t yet natively supported by SGLang. This is where transformers backend shines, enabling optimized inference without waiting for native support.

There are several key areas we are actively working on to enhance this integration:.

Performance Improvements: transformer models presently lag behind the native integration in terms of performance.Our primary objective is to optimize and narrow this gap.

VLM Integration: we are also working toward adding support for Vision-Language Models (VLM) to broaden the range of capabilities and use cases.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gemma 3n was announced as a preview during Google I/O. The on-device community got really excited, because this is a model designed from the ground up to run locally on your hardware. On top of that, it’s natively multimodal, supporting image, text, audio, and video inputs 🤯.

Today, Gemma 3n is finally available on the most used open source libraries. This includes transformers & timm, MLX, llama.cpp (text inputs), transformers.js, ollama, Google AI Edge, and others.

This post quickly goes through practical snippets to demonstrate how to use the model with these libraries, and how easy it is to fine-tune it for other domains.

Here is the Gemma 3n Release Collection.

Recent findings suggest that two model sizes have been released today, with two variants (base and instruct) each. The model names follow a non-standard nomenclature: they are called gemma-3n-E2B and gemma-3n-E4B. The E preceding the parameter count stands for Effective. Their actual parameter counts are 5B and 8B, respectively, but thanks to improvements in memory efficiency, they manage to only need 2B and 4B in VRAM (GPU memory).

These models, therefore, behave like 2B and 4B in terms of hardware support, but they punch over 2B/4B in terms of quality. The E2B model can run in as little as 2GB of GPU RAM, while E4B can run with just 3GB of GPU RAM.

According to recent reports, in addition to the language decoder, Gemma 3n uses an audio encoder and a vision encoder. We highlight their main features below, and describe how they have been added to transformers and timm, as they are the reference for other implementations.

It has been revealed that the easiest way to vibe check the model is with the dedicated Hugging Face Space for the model. You can try out different prompts, with different modalities, here.

Install the latest version of timm (for the vision encoder) and transformers to run inference, or if you want to fine tune it.

The easiest way to start using Gemma 3n is by using the pipeline abstraction in transformers:.

Initialize the model and the processor from the Hub, and write the model_generation function that takes care of processing the prompts and running the inference on the model.

Support for videos is done as a collection of frames of images.

Industry observers note that gemma 3n comes with day 0 support for MLX across all 3 modalities. Make sure to upgrade your mlx-vlm installation.

In addition to MLX, Gemma 3n (text only) works out of the box with llama.cpp. Make sure to install llama.cpp/ Ollama from source.

Check out the Installation instruction for llama.cpp here: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/install.md.

Sources indicate that finally, we are also releasing ONNX weights for the gemma-3n-E2B-it model variant, enabling flexible deployment across diverse runtimes and platforms. For JavaScript developers, Gemma3n has been integrated into Transformers.js and is available as of version 3.6.0.

For more information on how to run the model with these libraries, check out the usage section in the model card.

Given the size of the model, it’s pretty convenient to fine-tune it for specific downstream tasks across modalities. To make it easier for you to fine-tune the model, we’ve created a simple notebook that allows you to experiment on a free Google Colab!

We also provide a dedicated notebook for fine-tuning on audio tasks, so you can easily adapt the model to your speech datasets and benchmarks!

In a recent development, with this release, we also introduce the Hugging Face Gemma Recipes repository. One will find notebooks and scripts to run the models and fine tune them.

Recent findings suggest that we would love for you to use the Gemma family of models and add more recipes to it! Feel free to open Problems and create Pull Requests to the repository.

We are always excited to host Google and their Gemma family of models. We hope the community will get together and make the most of these models. Multimodal, small sized, and highly capable, make a great model release!

Recent findings suggest that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

You wrote a good email. You hit send. Then half your list never saw it, because it went straight to spam.

Sources indicate that that is a deliverability problem, and it costs more than most teams think. Every email that misses the inbox is a lead you paid for and never reached.

According to recent reports, the good part is that deliverability is not luck. Mailbox providers like Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook judge you on a short list of things: who you are, who you send to, and how people react. Fix those and your inbox placement goes up.

This guide covers 10 email deliverability best practices in the order you should fix them, starting with SPF and ending with sender reputation.

Email deliverability is the share of your emails that land in the inbox instead of the spam folder or nowhere at all.

It has been revealed that people often mix it up with delivery rate. They are not the same thing.

You can have a 99% delivery rate and still have most of your emails sitting in spam. That is why your email tool can say "delivered" while your open rate keeps dropping.

The substantial mailbox providers stopped treating authentication as optional.

It has been revealed that microsoft followed on May 5, 2025. If you send more than 5,000 emails a day to Outlook.com, Hotmail or Live addresses, you need all three records in place or your mail goes to junk.

Send less than 5,000 a day? Follow the rules anyway. The same checks decide inbox placement for small senders too, just without the public warning.

Sources indicate that SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a TXT record in your DNS. It lists the servers allowed to send email from your domain.

When your email arrives, the receiving server checks that list. If the sending server is not on it, the email looks suspicious.

A basic SPF record looks like this:.

Recent findings suggest that DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a digital signature to each email. The receiving server uses a public key in your DNS to check two things: the email came from you, and nobody changed it on the way.

Your email provider gives you the DKIM record. You paste it into your DNS and switch signing on.

DKIM also survives forwarding, which SPF does not. If you can only get one of the two perfect, get DKIM right.

DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together. It tells mailbox providers what to do when an email fails both checks, and it sends you reports on who is sending mail under your domain name.

Start with a monitoring policy:.

p=none means "take no action, just send me reports." It is the minimum Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft accept from bulk senders.

Don't stop there. Read the reports for a few weeks, fix any real sender that is failing, then move up:.

According to recent reports, one more thing: DMARC needs alignment. The domain in your From address has to match the domain used in SPF or DKIM. Plenty of senders have all three records and still fail DMARC because their email tool signs with its own domain.

If you'd rather not handle this in-house, you can also hire a B2B cold email marketing agency such as IntentSignal, Martal or Belkins. A good agency will set up the domains, mailboxes, warm-up and SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for you, and keep an eye on deliverability while the campaigns run.

A upcoming domain has no history. If it sends 10,000 emails on day one, it looks exactly like a spammer who just bought a domain.

Warm-up means starting small and growing a little each day, so mailbox providers can watch how people react to you.

A simple schedule for a new domain:.

Send to your most active contacts first. Their opens and replies are what build trust early. If bounces or complaints jump, hold at that volume until they settle.

Industry observers note that and if you run cold outreach, do it from a separate domain or subdomain. That way a bad campaign can't hurt the domain your invoices and password resets come from.

In a recent development, A bigger list is not a better list. Dead addresses and people who stopped caring pull your numbers down.

Never buy a list. Bought lists are full of spam traps, which are addresses that exist only to catch senders who email people without permission. Hitting a few of them can get your domain blocklisted.

Yes, you lose some sign-ups. What you keep is real people with working inboxes who actually want your emails. That means fewer bounces, fewer complaints and better opens from day one.

It also keeps bots and fake addresses out of your forms, which matters a lot if your sign-up form is public.

It has been revealed that most email platforms add these for you. Check that yours does.

These two numbers tell you the most about where you stand.

The complaint figures come from Gmail's own rules. The bounce figures are the working limits most email platforms use.

According to recent reports, A 0.3% complaint rate is only 3 complaints per 1,000 emails. It does not take much to cross that line.

If complaints are climbing, ask three questions:.

Most complaint problems come from one of those three, not from the email itself.

Spam filters got smarter. A single word like "free" won't sink you anymore. Patterns will.

Replies help a lot. When someone replies, the mailbox provider sees a real conversation. Ask a question in your welcome email and you'll get some.

Recent findings suggest that sender reputation is the score mailbox providers give your domain and IP. Everything above feeds into it. A good score means inbox. A bad one means spam, no matter how good the email is.

You can't see the exact score, but these free tools get you close:.

Check them weekly, and right after any big campaign.

A few habits protect your reputation over time:.

According to recent reports, aim for 95% or higher inbox placement. Below 90% means something needs fixing, usually authentication or list quality.

The common causes are missing or broken SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, a high complaint rate, an old list with lots of dead addresses, or a fresh domain that sent too much too soon. Check authentication first because it is the fastest to fix.

Industry observers note that DNS fixes like SPF and DKIM take effect within a day or two. Reputation is slower. Expect two to six weeks of steady, clean sending before inbox placement recovers.

Yes. The 5,000 mark is where Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft start enforcing openly. Small senders are still judged on the same signals, and Gmail asks every sender for at least SPF or DKIM.

Only if you send enough to keep it warm, roughly 100,000 emails a month or more. Below that, a good shared IP from a trusted provider usually performs better.

Sender reputation covers both your IP address and your domain. Domain reputation is the part tied to your domain name, and it follows you even if you switch email providers. Gmail leans on domain reputation more than IP.

If you only have an hour this week, spend it on SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Nothing else works until those pass.

It has been revealed that after that, clean your list and keep an eye on complaints. Send emails people asked for, to people who still want them, from a domain that proves who it is. Do that for a few weeks and your emails will land in the inbox again.
